analysis.one_liner: Bans unconscionably excessive gasoline prices during presidentially proclaimed oil-market emergencies.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in February 2023 with three cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Commerce Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to sell gasoline or other fuels at unconscionably excessive prices once the President declares a domestic or international crisis affecting oil markets, with each proclamation lasting up to 30 days and renewable. A price counts as gouging if it grossly exceeds what the seller charged before the crisis or what competitors charge, and is not explained by the seller's own added costs or risks. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban with stiff penalties — up to triple the profits gained or $100 million in civil fines, plus criminal fines up to $500 million for individuals or companies — prioritizing companies with over $10 billion in annual U.S. fuel sales, and state attorneys general could sue retailers in federal court on residents' behalf. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, farmers, and businesses that buy fuel at the pump or wholesale, who during an emergency would be protected from sellers charging far more than pre-crisis or market prices without a cost justification.

how_it_helps.text: During a proclaimed crisis, it would be unlawful to sell gasoline or any other petroleum distillate at a price that is unconscionably excessive and takes unfair advantage of the crisis. [S2] [S3]

A price is judged against what the seller charged in the prior 30 days, what competitors charged in the same area, and whether the increase genuinely reflected the seller's additional costs or risks. [S3]

The FTC would enforce the ban with civil penalties up to triple the violator's profits or $100 million, each day of a continuing violation counting separately, and would prioritize enforcement against companies with over $10 billion in annual U.S. fuel sales. [S3]
The Justice Department could seek criminal fines up to $500 million, also prioritizing the largest companies. [S3]
State attorneys general could bring federal court actions on behalf of their residents against retail price gouging, with their state laws untouched. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies and fuel retailers, who would face new federal and state legal exposure during every proclaimed emergency, and who could see legitimate cost-driven price increases challenged under a subjective standard; any penalties or compliance costs could ultimately be passed into fuel prices.

drawbacks.text: The standard — 'unconscionably excessive' and 'taking unfair advantage' — is inherently subjective, which could chill legitimate price increases that reflect genuinely higher wholesale costs or supply risks during a crisis. [S3]

Penalties could discourage fuel distributors from moving extra supply into a shortage area, since selling more at a higher market price raises the risk of being judged a gouger; the bill tries to limit this by weighing whether a seller increased supply after the proclamation, but the risk remains. [S3]
Enforcement depends entirely on the President choosing to declare an emergency, so the protection could be switched on or off for political rather than market reasons. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise is real: during the most acute shortages — hurricanes, refinery outages, war shocks — the bill would give federal and state enforcers a tool against sellers charging far above their own cost increases, aimed primarily at the largest companies. The design is reasonably targeted (it benchmarks against pre-crisis and competitor prices and excuses genuine cost increases), but the vague 'unconscionably excessive' standard and the presidential trigger are genuine weaknesses that an honest supporter would acknowledge. The bill never got far enough for these trade-offs to be tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in February 2023, and the committee never took it up; when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, the bill died with it.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Duckworth introduced the bill on February 9, 2023, joined by Sens. Blumenthal, Murray, and Warren as cosponsors. [S1] [S4]
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation — the only action it ever received. [S5]
The committee took no further action, and no version of the bill was ever reported, debated, or voted on in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil and gas companies and fuel retailers came out ahead: no federal anti-gouging statute was created, so they face no new penalties during future oil-market emergencies, and only whatever state-level gouging laws already exist apply.

for.name: Sen. Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Commerce Committee.

for.name: 3 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Sens. Blumenthal, Murray, Warren).

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or recorded floor opposition exist; the bill had only Democratic support (all four sponsors and cosponsors) and died quietly in committee, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Under the bill, the largest producers (over $10 billion in annual U.S. fuel sales) would have been the top enforcement priority, facing civil penalties up to triple profits or $100 million and criminal fines up to $500 million during declared emergencies. Their exposure would have been the public's protection, so the bill's defeat left them better off.

Wholesale and retail sales would both have been covered, and state attorneys general could sue retailers directly in federal court on residents' behalf. Small and mid-sized stations would also have faced new legal risk during emergencies, though federal enforcement would have focused on the giants.

Ordinary fuel buyers would have gained a federal backstop against emergency price spikes, enforceable by the FTC and by their own state attorneys general. As consumers rather than an industry, they are the bill's intended beneficiaries.
